summary.title: Literature review on the benefits of static types
summary.one_liner: Static typing studies mostly find small or context-dependent effects on software quality and developer productivity, and many of the studies have serious methodological flaws.
keywords: ansi c vs k&r c type checking
takeaways: Most empirical studies of static vs dynamic typing find very small effects, if any, on software quality.
Type checking of procedure interfaces (ANSI C vs K&R C) reduced interface defects in one controlled experiment.
Static types appeared to help with type-error tasks in Java vs Groovy, but not with semantic errors, and the tasks were trivial.
Individual programmer differences were often larger than differences between languages.
Many of the studies use student subjects, small samples, or unrealistic tasks, so they may not generalize to real-world contexts.
summary.summary: The author reviews a set of empirical studies on whether static type systems improve software quality, maintainability, and developer productivity. Each study is summarized with its abstract and a critical commentary on design, sample, and analysis. The GitHub-based study by Ray et al. is criticized for misclassified projects and weak causal inference, while controlled experiments by Hanenberg, Kleinschmager, Prechelt, and others are examined for small samples, trivial tasks, student subjects, and multiple comparisons. The overall conclusion is that the evidence shows small or context-dependent effects, and that the studies probably do not cover the contexts readers care about.
